  • USBGuard (/etc/usbguard/rules.conf) allows hubs and the devices whose interfaces are all mass storage; it blocks every other device, including a key that has a storage interface and another one. Blocked devices are listed in /var/log/usbguard/usbguard-audit.log, and the kiosk reports each one in its own log as a usb_device_blocked event, also sent to the SIEM (Refused USB devices).
  • No device is authorized before USBGuard has started: the kernel command line sets usbcore.authorized_default=0. If USBGuard does not start, no USB device is usable.
  • Drivers removed from the image (KernelModulesExclude= in image/mkosi.conf): USB network adapters, wireless, Bluetooth, USB serial adapters and modems, plus the staging drivers and batman-adv, which would bring the wireless modules back as dependencies. Such devices have no driver even if they were authorized.
  • USB HID is kept for the touchscreen of the reference hardware, a Waveshare 7-inch HDMI LCD (C), allowed by its own rule:
allow id 0eef:0005 serial "220211" name "WS170120" with-interface 03:00:00 via-port "1-8"

its USB touch controller (eGalax) with its single generic HID interface (a keyboard has 03:01:01), on the internal port of the enclosure, this unit only. A device that copies its identifiers on another port, or that adds a keyboard interface, is blocked; so is every keyboard and mouse. Another unit or port: adapt the rule to the line the audit log shows when it is blocked. The kernel (mousedev) turns a touch into a left click on /dev/input/mice, which the kiosk reads to confirm a cleaning.

The test image allows the touch tablet of the virtual machine (QEMU usb-tablet, same interface) in its own rule (/etc/usbguard/rules.d/50-vm-test.conf): the test confirms a cleaning with a touch. The keyboard of the virtual machines is not a USB device.

docs.title: Mouse instead of a touchscreen
docs.text:
With a screen that is not a touchscreen, a mouse confirms a cleaning: the kernel merges all mice in /dev/input/mice, and a left click is read as a touch. Nothing changes in the kiosk, but USBGuard blocks every mouse: allow yours by its own rule in image/mkosi.extra/etc/usbguard/rules.conf, then rebuild the image and write it again. The root file system is read-only and checked by dm-verity: a rule changed on the kiosk itself is not possible.

  1. Plug the mouse into the kiosk and take its line from /var/log/usbguard/usbguard-audit.log, or from usb-devices.txt of a maintenance export: its id, name, serial (when it has one) and port.

  2. Add a rule that allows this mouse, with only a mouse interface (03:01:02), on the port where it is plugged, for example:

    allow id 046d:c077 name "USB Optical Mouse" with-interface equals { 03:01:02 } via-port "1-5"

    Add serial "..." when the mouse has a serial number: the rule then allows this unit only.

Choose a simple wired mouse. Many wireless mice (receivers shared with a keyboard) and gaming mice also have a keyboard interface (03:01:01): equals keeps them blocked, so that a keyboard cannot pass for a mouse. Keep the mouse on the port of the rule. Edit the file with LF line endings: the build refuses a file with CRLF line endings.

docs.title: System hardening
docs.text:
After the ANSSI configuration recommendations for GNU/Linux systems:

  • Kernel settings (/usr/lib/sysctl.d/90-pandora-box.conf): kernel logs and addresses hidden, no ptrace, no kexec, no unprivileged eBPF, user namespaces or userfaultfd, io_uring disabled, no SysRq, no core dumps, protected links and FIFOs, no IP forwarding or redirects.
  • Kernel command line: memory initialized on allocation and free, no slab merging, randomized page allocator and kernel stack, no legacy vsyscall, no debugfs, lockdown in confidentiality mode (Secure Boot only enables integrity: even root cannot read kernel memory), IOMMU in strict mode and no DMA before the kernel starts (DMA attacks through ports).
  • Firewall (/etc/nftables.conf): every packet is dropped, in and out, except on the loopback interface.
  • No login: no login console on the screens (getty@ and getty-static disabled), no login program, no root password, Ctrl-Alt-Del masked.
  • clamd sandbox (clamav-daemon.service.d/50-pandora-box.conf): no network, read-only system, no device, system call filter, MemoryDenyWriteExecute (the Debian clamd interprets bytecode signatures, without JIT); it runs as the clamav user.
  • Kiosk service (packaging/systemd/pandora-box.service): read-only system, system call filter, limited capabilities. It keeps AF_NETLINK (udev events), the capabilities needed to start the worker sandbox (namespaces, change of user, loopback interface of the workers) and cannot have MemoryDenyWriteExecute or RestrictSUIDSGID: the first one would also apply to the YARA-X workers, which compile rules to native code, the second one refuses a system call bubblewrap needs.
  • Kernel modules removed: network protocols the kiosk never uses (DCCP, SCTP, RDS, TIPC) and FireWire, another way to reach the memory of the kiosk, besides the USB network, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi drivers, and the NTFS and exFAT drivers (read in user space, see Filesystem drivers). The protocols, FireWire, NTFS and exFAT are also listed in /etc/modprobe.d/pandora-box.conf, where the auditing tools look for them.
  • Audit log (/etc/audit/audit.rules, auditd): loading of kernel modules, mounts (except those of systemd and bubblewrap), every program started, ptrace, changes of the clock, of the signature sets and of the staged image updates. The rules are locked (-e 2): changing them needs a reboot. They are loaded by auditctl -R (augenrules writes into /etc, read-only). The log is in /var/log/audit/audit.log, for instance ausearch -k signatures -i.

The test profile includes lynis, run by the automated test: hardening index 73, no warnings. Its remaining suggestions do not apply to a kiosk without login (password policy, banners, package tools, fail2ban) or come later (remote logging, phase 5).

docs.title: Scan worker sandbox
docs.text:
The scan workers parse hostile files with several engines (libmagic, YARA-X, the clamd client...): they are assumed compromisable (scan.sandbox, src/pandora_box/sandbox.py).

  • One engine per worker: a compromised engine (a crafted file exploiting YARA-X or libmagic) cannot forge the result of another engine. The kiosk hashes each file itself, asks the worker of each hash engine (MalwareBazaar, Hashlookup) with the hashes only, then passes the file to a worker of each content engine (ClamAV, YARA-X), and combines their results itself; a worker only reports the result of its own engine. Content engines have scan.workers workers each, hash engines one. scan.workers = "auto" (the default) scans one file per CPU at the same time, as many as the memory allows (1.5 GB for clamd and the system, then 256 MB each, for the YARA rules mostly): 6 on the ThinkCentre M720q (6 cores, 8 GB), 1 or 2 on a computer with 2 GB.
  • No access to the device: the kiosk opens each file safely (no link followed, the file of the inventory) and passes the open descriptor to the workers of the content engines, which never open a file of the device; the workers of the hash engines never get the file.
  • bubblewrap: new PID, IPC, UTS, cgroup and network namespaces (no network interface but loopback); a file system holding only /usr, a few files of /etc, the signature folders of the enabled engines (read-only), the YARA-X cache and the clamd socket folder: no device mount point, no reports, quarantine, logs or configuration.
  • Dedicated user pandora-box-scan (packaging/sysusers/), switched to by setpriv: no capability, no supplementary group, no_new_privs.
  • System call filter (src/pandora_box/seccomp.py), installed once the engines are loaded: no program execution, debugging, mounts, namespaces, eBPF, kernel modules, io_uring, network sockets...
  • Untrusted answers: workers answer in JSON (never pickle), limited in size and validated (src/pandora_box/protocol.py); the path and size of the file always come from the kiosk. A malformed answer kills the worker and the file is reported as an error.

bubblewrap runs as root (the kiosk service), so unprivileged user namespaces stay disabled.

The virtual machine test checks these settings and prints the exposure of the services measured by systemd-analyze security (0 to 10, lower is better): about 1.6 for clamd, 3.8 for the kiosk (which starts the worker sandbox), 2.8 for USBGuard.

docs.title: Filesystem drivers
docs.text:
A kernel filesystem driver parses the structures written on the key: a flaw of this driver, on a crafted key, runs code in the kernel, before any sandbox (the NTFS, exFAT and ext4 drivers of Linux get regular fuzzing findings). NTFS, exFAT and ext4 are therefore read by a FUSE driver, in the sandbox of the scan workers (device.fuse, src/pandora_box/fuse.py):

Filesystem Driver vfat kernel (its simplest and oldest driver) exFAT exfat-fuse NTFS ntfs-3g ext4 fuse2fs
  • No privilege: the kiosk opens /dev/fuse and mounts the connection itself (noexec,nosuid,nodev, read-only to scan); the driver only serves it. libfuse 3 drivers take the mounted connection as mount point /dev/fd/N; ntfs-3g carries its own FUSE library, which mounts by itself: a library preloaded into ntfs-3g only (packaging/fuse/premounted.c) hands it the connection. fusermount3 is not setuid.
  • Sandbox: the bubblewrap sandbox of the workers, as the pandora-box-scan user with the group of the block device, without capabilities. The block device is its only device; it sees /usr, the user names and nothing of the kiosk.
  • Watchdog: a driver that crashed makes every access fail; a driver whose requests stay unanswered while the key reads nothing is killed after device.command_timeout. Either way the key is reported not verified. Once the key is unmounted, the kiosk waits for the driver to exit: it writes its last changes (cleaning).
  • Kernel drivers removed: the image has no NTFS and exFAT kernel modules; ext4 stays for the data partition.

A compromised driver no longer takes over the kiosk, but it can still hide files from the scan. fuse2fs refuses an ext4 key whose journal needs a replay, like the kernel.

docs.title: Unified kernel image
docs.text: The UKI (about 40 MB) holds the kernel, the initrd of the image (image/mkosi.images/initrd/, without the udev hardware database, charset conversions, Perl, documentation and networkd) and an initrd of kernel modules. That one only holds what mounts the root filesystem (KernelModulesInitrdInclude= in image/mkosi.conf): disk controllers (NVMe, SATA, Intel VMD, eMMC, virtio), dm-verity, EROFS and CRC32C, which EROFS loads by name. The other modules are loaded from the root filesystem. A computer whose disk controller is not in this list cannot find its root filesystem: add its module there.

docs.title: Initial installation
docs.text: A kiosk is installed once: the BIOS is configured, the image is written to its disk, Secure Boot is locked to the image key at the first boot, then a first signature set is installed from a USB key. Afterwards it is only updated with signed USB keys or online (Maintenance).

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
1. Build the image: Building the image.
  2. Configure the BIOS: supervisor password, Secure Boot in setup mode, boot from the internal disk only.
  3. Write the image to the disk of the kiosk.
  4. First boot: the image enrolls its Secure Boot key; check that Secure Boot is in User mode.
  5. Insert a first signature set: until then, the kiosk shows NO VALID SIGNATURES and scans nothing.
  6. Check the kiosk with a test key and a maintenance device.

The settings below are those of the validated hardware, a Lenovo ThinkCentre M720q Tiny (see Hardware).

docs.title: BIOS configuration
docs.text: The settings of the ThinkCentre M720q (press F1 at power on). The names are those of the Lenovo BIOS of this generation and may vary slightly with the version; the goal of each setting matters more than its exact name.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Setting Value Why Security → Supervisor Password set, kept by the operator nobody changes the boot order, Secure Boot or the settings below Security → Power-On Password none the kiosk starts by itself after a power failure Security → Secure Boot → Secure Boot Enabled the firmware only starts the signed boot loader of the image Security → Secure Boot → Secure Boot Mode Custom, then Reset to Setup Mode (or Clear All Secure Boot Keys) at its first boot, the image enrolls its own certificate (loader/keys/auto): the computer then only starts PandoraBox images Security → Device Guard / Intel TXT default not used Security → Chassis Intrusion Detection Enabled, if the enclosure has the switch an opened kiosk is reported at the next start

Enrolling only the image certificate also refuses the option ROMs signed by Microsoft: fine with the integrated Intel graphics of the M720q, but a computer that needs an add-in graphics card or disk controller would not start it.

docs.title: Startup
docs.text: Setting Value Why Startup → Boot Mode UEFI only the image only boots in UEFI mode Startup → Primary Boot Sequence the internal SSD only the kiosk never starts from a USB key inserted by a user Startup → USB Boot Disabled same Startup → PXE / Network Boot Disabled no start from the network Startup → Boot Menu (F12) Disabled, if offered no other boot device chosen at power on (the supervisor password protects it otherwise) Startup → Fast Boot default

docs.title: Devices and advanced settings
docs.text: Setting Value Why Advanced → CPU Setup → Intel Virtualization Technology for Directed I/O (VT-d) Enabled the IOMMU protects the memory against DMA from devices (the kernel uses it in strict mode) Devices → Network Setup → Wake on LAN Disabled Devices → USB Setup the ports not used by the users or the touchscreen disabled, if the BIOS offers it per port fewer ways in (physical hardening) Devices → Audio / Serial / Card reader Disabled when present not used

docs.title: Power
docs.text: Setting Value Why Power → After Power Loss Power On the kiosk starts again after a power failure

docs.title: Writing the image
docs.text:
The SSD is written once, from another computer (in a USB enclosure):

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,TRAN          # the disk of the SSD, e.g. /dev/sdX
sudo umount /dev/sdX?*                 # if partitions were mounted automatically
sudo dd if=image/mkosi.output/pandora-box.raw of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress

Caution

Check the disk name twice: dd overwrites the whole disk.

The image can be written to a disk of any size: at every boot, the data partition (/var) grows to fill the disk.

docs.title: First boot
docs.text:
Put the SSD back in the kiosk and start it. With the firmware in Secure Boot setup mode, systemd-boot enrolls the certificate of the image in place of the Microsoft keys (PK, KEK and db, from loader/keys/auto/ on the ESP), then the kiosk starts. From then on, the computer only starts images signed with the same key.

After this first boot, check in the BIOS that Secure Boot is on: it shows the mode User. To give the computer back to another use: Security → Secure Boot → Restore Factory Keys.

The boot loader has no menu and does not read the keyboard: there is no way to choose another system or to open a session on the kiosk.

docs.title: First signature set
docs.text:
A new kiosk has no signature set: it shows NO VALID SIGNATURES and only accepts a signature update device. Prepare one on the computer that holds the update key, and insert it (see Signatures):

export ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY=...
publish/publish.sh /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures image/update.key
cp -r /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures /media/$USER/KEY/

The kiosk verifies and installs the set, loads its engines, asks to remove the key, then waits for a key to scan. A kiosk built with the profile online and connected to the network also downloads its signatures itself, 5 minutes after boot (Online updates).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Insert a key holding the EICAR test file: the kiosk reports it, and removes it after a touch of the screen.
  • The touchscreen confirms a cleaning. If it does not, USBGuard blocks it: its rule is tied to the serial number and port of the touch controller (USB devices).
  • Bring the logs back with a maintenance device: failed-services.txt is empty, signatures.txt shows the installed set.

docs.title: Kiosk interface
docs.text:
The kiosk shows what it does on its touch screen: waiting for a key, scan progress, the dangerous files found, then the result. There are no buttons: the only action of the user is a touch anywhere on the screen to start the cleaning, once the files to remove are listed.

Waiting for a key Scan in progress Threats found: touch to clean Key cleaned

docs.title: Screens
docs.text:
Screen When ready Waiting for a key (animation of a key inserted), with the versions of the kiosk and of its signatures unavailable No valid signatures: the kiosk only accepts a signature update device scanning Device, progress bar, files scanned out of the total, threats found so far, the latest files scanned and their verdict threats The files that will be removed, with their detection; a touch on the screen cleans the key cleaning The files being removed clean No threat found: the key can be used warning Suspicious or not fully scanned files are kept (scan.suspicious or scan.on_error set to warn) cleaned The removed files not_cleaned The files that could not be removed, or the key was removed before the cleaning not_verified Files that could not be scanned (scan.on_error = "block"): the key must not be used error The key could not be mounted or read service Maintenance, signature or image update device: the messages of the kiosk

A result (scan, maintenance or update device) stays on the screen until the key is removed, then display.return_seconds more (5 seconds by default) before the waiting screen. Inserting another key shows its scan at once.

docs.title: How it is drawn
docs.text:
The screens are drawn with Pillow and copied into the Linux framebuffer (display.framebuffer, /dev/fb0): no display server, no browser, nothing that listens on a socket. The kiosk puts its console (tty1) in graphics mode, so that the kernel does not draw text over the screens. Touches are read from /dev/input/mice (the touch screen is seen as a mouse; a mouse allowed by USBGuard clicks instead, see image.md), only while the kiosk waits for the cleaning to be confirmed. File names and device labels come from the key: they are made printable (control and invisible formatting characters replaced) and cut to their place, never interpreted. The graphical interface needs a 24 or 32 bits per pixel framebuffer (Intel, efifb, QEMU).

The configuration selects it with kiosk.interface = "framebuffer" (the default); curses is the text interface (administrator mode), console prints plain text (development).

docs.title: Customization
docs.text: An administrator adapts the interface to the organization: logo, colors, texts of every screen and their language, images. The image is read-only (dm-verity): the theme is part of it, and a change needs a new image (or an image update).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
In packaging/pandora-box.toml, section [display]:

[display]
# Theme folder, installed in the image from image/theme/
theme = "/usr/share/pandora-box/theme"
# Language of the texts: "en", "fr", "de", "nl", or a language the theme adds
language = "fr"
# Seconds before the waiting screen, once the key is removed
return_seconds = 5.0

docs.title: Theme folder
docs.text:
Create image/theme/ in the repository: the image build copies it to /usr/share/pandora-box/theme and checks it (the build fails on an invalid theme). The folder holds a theme.toml and the files it names. Every key is optional: a key of the theme replaces the one of the built-in theme (src/pandora_box/ui/theme/theme.toml, which lists them all), the others are kept.

image/theme/
├── theme.toml
└── logo.png

# Logo of the organization, on the left of the header (PNG or JPEG)
logo = "logo.png"
# TrueType fonts, files of the folder (default: DejaVu Sans)
# font = "OpenSans-Regular.ttf"
# font_bold = "OpenSans-Bold.ttf"
# Larger texts, from 1 (default) to 1.5
# text_scale = 1.25

[colors]
header = "#003366"
progress = "#003366"

[texts.fr]
title = "Hôpital de Mons - Borne antivirus"
footer = "Service informatique - poste 1234"
insert_help = "Analysez toute clé USB avant de l'utiliser sur un poste de l'hôpital."
clean_help = "Cette clé peut être utilisée. N'oubliez pas de la retirer."

docs.title: Texts
docs.text:
Every text shown on the screen is a key of [texts.<language>]: the title of the header, the footer, the title and the help of each screen, the verdicts of the files. Some texts have placeholders, replaced by the kiosk:

Text Placeholders scan_progress {done}, {total} scan_threats, cleaned_help, more_files {count} device_usage {size}, {used}

A text with an unknown placeholder or an unknown key is refused. English (en), French (fr), German (de) and Dutch (nl) are built in; a theme may change some of their texts, or add a language: [texts.it] with the texts it translates, the others are in English; then set display.language = "it".

The messages of the service, error, unavailable and cleaning screens are those of the kiosk logs (in English): they are meant for the administrator, and are not part of the theme.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: header, header_text, background, text, muted (help, details), clean, threat, warning, progress, progress_background: "#rrggbb". A theme whose texts would be hard to read is refused (see Accessibility).

docs.title: Images
docs.text: [images]: insert (animation of the waiting screen, one image per second), busy (animation while the kiosk works), clean, threat, error (icons of the results). PNG (with transparency) or JPEG, at most 4096 pixels. The built-in images come from the first version of PandoraBox.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
• Contrast: every text must stand out from its background at the WCAG 2.1 AA level, or the theme is refused with the colors and ratio at fault: 4.5:1 for text, muted, clean, threat and warning on background; 3:1 for header_text on header, threat and progress (large bold texts: title, banner, percentage) and for progress on progress_background (the progress bar). The built-in theme passes.
  • Text size: text_scale enlarges every text, from 1 (default) to 1.5; the lines, rows and bars follow, the icons and the animation of the waiting screen shrink to make room. The smallest built-in text is 16 pixels on the 7-inch screen (1024x600). Long titles wrap; when space runs short, a list always shows its first file and the number of the others. The tests check every screen in English, French, German and Dutch, at three screen sizes and three text sizes: no text leaves the screen or overlaps another one.
  • No color alone: each result has its title, its icon and, for each file, its verdict in words; the whole screen is the button to clean.

To try a text size without changing the theme: pandora-box-theme preview image/theme /tmp/preview --text-scale 1.5.

docs.title: Check and preview a theme
docs.text:
Without a kiosk, on the development computer:

pandora-box-theme check image/theme
pandora-box-theme preview image/theme /tmp/preview            # every language
pandora-box-theme preview image/theme /tmp/preview --language fr --size 800x480

preview draws every screen, with made-up files, into PNG files. pandora-box --check-config also checks the theme of the configuration.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: A kiosk has no login and accepts no connection: its logs are brought back with a signed maintenance device, or sent as they are logged to a SIEM by an online kiosk.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY            # any kiosk
image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY kiosk-1    # only kiosk.name = kiosk-1

Insert the key into the kiosk: it writes its logs to pandora-box-maintenance/<kiosk>-<date>/ and ejects the key.

For a continuous export, see Log export to a SIEM.

docs.title: What the kiosk logs
docs.text:
Log Path on the kiosk Content Kiosk /var/log/pandora-box/pandora-box.log JSON lines: devices inserted and removed, USB devices refused by USBGuard, scans and their verdicts, infected files, quarantine and cleaning, signature and image updates, maintenance devices, errors Scan reports /var/lib/pandora-box/reports/ One JSON report per scanned device (see Scan report) Quarantine /var/lib/pandora-box/quarantine/ Copies of the infected files removed from the keys Journal journalctl System, services and kernel; one folder per boot, within the journald size limits USBGuard /var/log/usbguard/usbguard-audit.log Devices allowed and blocked Audit /var/log/audit/audit.log Kernel modules loaded, mounts, programs started, ptrace, changes of the clock, of the signature sets and of the staged image updates

Every entry of the kiosk log holds timestamp, level, kiosk (kiosk.name) and event, then the fields of the event. The level is set by logging.level (INFO by default). logrotate moves the log file every month and keeps 12 months, compressed.

Everything is on the data partition (/var), kept across reboots and image updates.

docs.title: Maintenance device
docs.text:
A maintenance device brings the logs of a kiosk back without taking its disk out. On the computer that holds the update key, with a USB key mounted:

image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY            # any kiosk
image/maintenance-key.sh /media/$USER/KEY kiosk-1    # only kiosk.name = kiosk-1

writes pandora-box-maintenance/ on the key: a request signed with the update key, valid 7 days. Inserted into the kiosk, even one without signatures, the key is not scanned: the kiosk verifies the request, writes its logs to pandora-box-maintenance/<kiosk>-<date>/ and ejects the key (src/pandora_box/maintenance.py).

File Content pandora-box.log Log of the kiosk journal.txt, journal-previous-boot.txt Journal of the boot and of the previous one kernel.txt Kernel messages boots.txt, boot-entries.txt Boots, installed versions of the image (System updates) services.txt, failed-services.txt systemd units, failed units usbguard-audit.log, usb-devices.txt, usb-rules.txt USB devices allowed and blocked, rules disks.txt Disks and partitions hardware.txt, cpuinfo.txt, meminfo.txt, input-devices.txt Hardware and screens, input devices os-release.txt, cmdline.txt Version of the image, kernel command line signatures.txt Installed signature set

Nothing changes on the kiosk, and the export holds no key, credential or scan report. A request signed by another key, too old, for another kiosk or modified is refused (maintenance_refused in the log).

One key can hold a maintenance request, a signature set (pandora-box-signatures/) and an image update (pandora-box-image/): the kiosk handles them in that order in one insertion, each verified on its own; the export shows the kiosk before the updates, and the image update comes last as it restarts the kiosk.

docs.title: Useful events
docs.text: Event Meaning device_verdict Summary of the scan of a device: verdict, counts, duration, detections, report_id (see Dashboards) infected_files Dangerous files found on a device signatures_installed, signatures_refused, signatures_not_newer Result of a signature update device signatures_changed New signature set loaded after an online update maintenance_refused Maintenance request refused usb_device_blocked USB device refused by USBGuard (see Refused USB devices) airgap_copied, airgap_failed, airgap_refused Copy of a key to a server (see Copy to a server) display_started, display_resized Size of the screen the interface draws for

docs.title: Refused USB devices
docs.text:
USBGuard blocks every USB device that is not only storage: a keyboard, a mouse, a network adapter, a key that is also a keyboard (BadUSB, see USB devices). Its audit log is readable only by root and is not sent to the SIEM: the kiosk follows it (src/pandora_box/usbguard.py) and logs each refused device in its own log, with the other events, as usb_device_blocked (level WARNING):

Field Content target Decision of USBGuard: block (or reject) usb_id Vendor and product identifiers, vendor:product model, serial Name and serial number the device gives port USB port, e.g. 1-2 interfaces Interfaces of the device, class:subclass:protocol kinds What these interfaces are: storage, keyboard, mouse, hid, communications (network, modem), wireless (Bluetooth), vendor-specific... composite true for a storage device with another function: a key that is also a keyboard connect_type hotplug when inserted, else present at boot or internal system_name Path of the device in sysfs rule Device rule of USBGuard, to adapt into an allow rule (touchscreen, mouse) blocked_at Time of the decision of USBGuard

Devices blocked before the kiosk starts (at boot) are reported once it has started; the position of the last line read is saved (/var/lib/pandora-box/usbguard-audit.json), so a restart of the kiosk reports no device twice. On a station, model, serial and rule are left out.

A device the operator meant to use (a mouse) appears here too; a key refused as a whole (composite), or a keyboard or a network adapter on a kiosk that has none, deserves a look.

docs.title: Export to a SIEM
docs.text: An online kiosk can send every entry of its log to a SIEM (Wazuh, Elastic, Graylog, Splunk, or any syslog server), over syslog or JSON, TLS, TCP or UDP: see Log export to a SIEM.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
A release of PandoraBox is a ready-to-write image published on GitHub, signed with the release keys of the project. A kiosk installed from it only starts images signed with the same Secure Boot key, and only installs the signature sets, image updates and maintenance requests signed with the same update key.

An organization that wants its own keys builds its image itself (Building the image): its kiosks then trust its keys, not those of the project.

docs.title: Release keys
docs.text:
Key Algorithm YubiKey slot Signs Public part Secure Boot key RSA 2048 9c systemd-boot, the unified kernel image, the dm-verity root hash; enrolled in the firmware of the kiosk image/release/secure-boot.crt Update key Ed25519 82 signature sets, image updates, maintenance requests, checksums of a release image/release/update.pem

The private keys never leave a YubiKey 5 (PIV application, firmware 5.7 or newer for Ed25519). The build container uses them through ykcs11 and the OpenSSL PKCS#11 provider (image/pkcs11.sh). It reaches the YubiKey through the PC/SC daemon of the build computer when one runs and answers it (/run/pcscd), else it starts its own, with the USB devices. The client of the container (pcsc-lite 2, Debian 13) does not talk to an older daemon (Debian 12): stop that one while signing, as it holds the YubiKey (sudo systemctl stop pcscd.socket pcscd); the scripts say so.

Two YubiKeys of the 5 series are needed (5 NFC, 5C NFC, 5 Nano…). The firmware of a YubiKey cannot be updated: check that it is 5.7 or newer before buying. The Security Key by Yubico models only have FIDO, not PIV: they cannot hold the keys. ykman info (package yubikey-manager, on the build computer) gives the model, the firmware and the applications enabled over USB; ykman config usb --enable PIV enables PIV when it is turned off.

The public parts are committed in image/release/. Their fingerprints are also published here, so that a release can be checked against a source other than itself:

openssl x509 -in image/release/secure-boot.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256
openssl pkey -pubin -in image/release/update.pem -outform DER | sha256sum

Important

The release keys are not created yet: the fingerprints will be given here.

docs.title: Creating the keys
docs.text:
Once, on an offline computer. The keys are created in memory, imported into two YubiKeys, the second one kept in a safe, then erased. A lost Secure Boot key means that the kiosks can only be installed again, by hand; a lost update key, that they get no more signature sets.

In the build container, with the files in memory only. The container uses its own PC/SC daemon: stop the one of the computer first, if it runs one (sudo systemctl stop pcscd.socket pcscd, sudo systemctl start pcscd.socket afterwards).

docker run --rm -it --device /dev/bus/usb -v /run/udev:/run/udev:ro \
    -v "$PWD/image/release:/release" --tmpfs /keys:mode=0700 pandora-box-builder bash
pcscd
opensc-tool -l      # lists the reader of the YubiKey: Yubico YubiKey ... CCID
cd /keys
openssl req -new -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 3650 -subj "/CN=PandoraBox release Secure Boot key/" \
    -keyout secure-boot.key -out secure-boot.crt
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out update.key
openssl req -new -x509 -key update.key -days 3650 -subj "/CN=PandoraBox release update key/" -out update.crt
openssl pkey -in update.key -pubout -out update.pem

Then for each YubiKey (-k asks for its management key; change the default PIN, PUK and management key of a new YubiKey first):

yubico-piv-tool -k -a import-key -s 9c -i secure-boot.key --pin-policy=once --touch-policy=never
yubico-piv-tool -k -a import-certificate -s 9c -i secure-boot.crt
yubico-piv-tool -k -a import-key -s 82 -i update.key --pin-policy=once --touch-policy=never
yubico-piv-tool -k -a import-certificate -s 82 -i update.crt
pkcs11-tool --module /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libykcs11.so --login --list-objects

ykcs11 only shows the key of a slot that holds a certificate. The PIN policy once lets one build sign every part of the image with a single PIN; the touch policy never, without touching the YubiKey at each signature.

Finally, publish the public keys and leave the container, which erases the private keys:

cp secure-boot.crt update.pem /release/
exit
git add image/release/secure-boot.crt image/release/update.pem

With other slots or another token, give the PKCS#11 URIs of the keys and the module: PANDORA_BOX_SECURE_BOOT_KEY, PANDORA_BOX_UPDATE_KEY and PANDORA_BOX_PKCS11_MODULE (see image/pkcs11.sh).

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text:
On the build computer, with the YubiKey plugged in and gh logged in to GitHub:

git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "PandoraBox 1.0.0"
git push origin v1.0.0
image/release.sh v1.0.0

image/release.sh asks for the PIN of the YubiKey once, then:

  1. extracts the files of the tag only (git archive) to release/v1.0.0/src/: no local theme, credentials or development keys get into the image;
  2. builds the image without profile, signed with the Secure Boot key (image/build.sh --release), trusting image/release/update.pem, with the inputs of a reproducible build;
  3. checks the signature of the unified kernel image, builds the signed image update, compresses the disk image, writes the software bill of materials, signs the checksums with the update key, and checks every signature with the public keys of the tag;
  4. creates a draft release of the tag on GitHub with the files of release/v1.0.0/assets/.
File Content pandora-box-v1.0.0.raw.xz disk image, to write to the disk of the kiosk pandora-box-image-v1.0.0.tar signed image update: pandora-box-image/, to extract at the root of a USB key (System updates) pandora-box-v1.0.0.cdx.json software bill of materials (SBOM, CycloneDX 1.5): the Debian and Python packages of the image, with their versions secure-boot.crt, update.pem public release keys SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.sig checksums, signed with the update key

Check the draft on GitHub, then publish it. --no-publish stops before GitHub. The image of a release has no profile: the profile online holds the credentials and settings of an organization, and is not published.

docs.title: Testing without a YubiKey
docs.text:
image/softhsm-keys.sh creates a SoftHSM token, a folder, with test keys in the slots and labels of the YubiKey:

image/softhsm-keys.sh /tmp/token
cp /tmp/token/secure-boot.crt /tmp/token/update.pem image/release/   # in a test clone only
echo 123456 | PANDORA_BOX_SOFTHSM=/tmp/token image/release.sh v0.0.0-test --no-publish

docs.title: Reproducing a release
docs.text:
The image of a release only depends on its tag: anyone can build it again and check that it is made of the published source code and Debian packages. image/reproducible.sh derives every input of the build from the tag:

Input Value Debian packages, and the tools of the build container snapshot.debian.org at the time of the tag Time of the files (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH), image version the time of the tag Partition UUIDs, dm-verity salt a seed derived from the commit Python packages pinned with their hashes (image/requirements.txt)

To check a release, download its files and build its tag again:

gh release download v1.0.0 -D /tmp/v1.0.0
image/reproduce.sh v1.0.0 /tmp/v1.0.0

image/reproduce.sh checks the files with their signed checksums, builds the tag with the same inputs, trusting the same update key, but signed with development keys, then compares:

Part Expected root filesystem, dm-verity hash tree identical unified kernel image every section identical, the kernel without its Secure Boot signatures (Debian's and the image's) software bill of materials identical

The signatures cannot be compared: they need the release keys, and hold the time they were made. They are checked with the public keys instead (Verifying a release). mkosi 25.3 is patched in the build container (image/patch-mkosi.py) so that the microcode of the kernel image is reproducible.

docs.title: Verifying a release
docs.text:
Download the files of the release, then check the signature of the checksums with the update key of the project, and the files with the checksums:

openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey update.pem -rawin -in SHA256SUMS -sigfile SHA256SUMS.sig
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
openssl pkey -pubin -in update.pem -outform DER | sha256sum

The last fingerprint must be the one given above: the update.pem of a release alone proves nothing, as anyone publishing a fake release would give their own. Then write the image (Initial installation):

xz -dc pandora-box-v1.0.0.raw.xz | sudo dd of=/dev/sdX bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress

At its first boot, the kiosk enrolls secure-boot.crt in its firmware. A kiosk installed with development keys does not accept the updates of a release: write the release image to its disk again.

docs.title: Log export to a SIEM
docs.text: The kiosk logs every event to a JSON lines file, /var/log/pandora-box/pandora-box.log: devices inserted and removed, scans and their verdicts, infected files, quarantine and cleaning, signature and image updates, maintenance devices, errors. An online kiosk can send these entries to a SIEM (Wazuh, Elastic, Graylog, Splunk, or any syslog server), as they are logged.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The export is off by default. It needs the image profile online (Building the image), which brings the network and the pandora-box-siem service, and the [siem] section of the configuration (packaging/pandora-box.toml):

[siem]
enabled = true
host = "siem.example.org"
# "tls" (default), "tcp" or "udp"
transport = "tls"
# 0: 6514 for tls, 514 for tcp and udp
port = 0
# Certificate authorities of the SIEM certificate, for tls ("": those of the
# system)
ca = "/usr/share/pandora-box/siem-ca.pem"
# "syslog" (RFC 5424) or "json"
format = "syslog"
facility = "local0"

pandora-box --check-config checks the section. The certificate authorities are part of the image: put them in image/siem-ca.pem (PEM), installed as /usr/share/pandora-box/siem-ca.pem when the image is built.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Each log entry is one message.

format = "syslog": an RFC 5424 message whose header comes from the entry, and whose message is the JSON entry itself:

<132>1 2026-10-14T10:25:32.123456+00:00 kiosk-01 pandora-box - infected_files - {"timestamp": "2026-10-14T10:25:32.123456+00:00", "level": "WARNING", "kiosk": "kiosk-01", "event": "infected_files", "count": 2}
Field Value PRI facility and the level of the entry: DEBUG 7, INFO 6, WARNING 4, ERROR 3 TIMESTAMP Time of the entry (UTC) HOSTNAME kiosk.name (characters other than printable ASCII replaced by _) APP-NAME pandora-box MSGID Name of the event (device_verdict, infected_files...)

Over TCP and TLS, the messages are framed by octet counting (RFC 5425, RFC 6587), as syslog over TLS requires.

format = "json": the JSON entry alone, one per line over TCP and TLS, one per datagram over UDP. This suits receivers of JSON lines (Logstash json_lines, Fluent Bit, Vector) and SIEMs that decode the JSON of a raw message.

Every entry holds timestamp, level, kiosk and event, then the fields of the event. The timestamps come from the clock of the kiosk, synchronized by NTP in the profile online (Time).

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: The statistics of a fleet of kiosks (keys scanned, verdicts, detections, cleanings, state of the signatures) are computed by the SIEM from the entries it receives: nothing to install on the kiosks. It is the same work in every SIEM: decode the JSON of the entry into fields, then count the events below. format = "json" is the simplest: the message is the JSON entry alone; with format = "syslog", it is the message part (MSG) of the syslog message.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event When Fields device_verdict Once per scanned key: the summary to count report_id, verdict (clean, malicious, suspicious, not_verified), complete, files, infected, suspicious, not_scanned, duration (seconds), used (bytes), detections (list of engine: name) device_cleaned The key was cleaned report_id, removed, infected airgap_copied, airgap_received, airgap_refused, airgap_failed Copy to and from a server (Copy to a server) report_id, counts, status kiosk_started Start of the kiosk image_version, signature_set, engines, signatures signatures_installed, signatures_changed New signature set serial, created file_scanned Each file (many entries) verdict, detail, engines, path usb_device_blocked A USB device refused by USBGuard: keyboard, network adapter, key that is also a keyboard (Refused USB devices) usb_id, model, serial, port, interfaces, kinds, composite, rule

Every entry also holds timestamp and kiosk (kiosk.name). report_id ties the events of a key together, and to its scan report. device_verdict never holds a name of a file; file_scanned and device_inserted hold the names of the files and the label and serial number of the key, usb_device_blocked the name and serial number of the device (left out on a station): drop them in the SIEM when they are not needed.

docs.title: Indicators
docs.text: Indicator From Keys scanned, per day and per kiosk count of device_verdict Verdicts device_verdict by verdict Most frequent detections detections of device_verdict, one value each Keys not verified (to look at) device_verdict with verdict = not_verified Keys cleaned count of device_cleaned, removed Scan time duration of device_verdict (average, 95th percentile) Signature set of each kiosk latest serial of signatures_installed / signatures_changed, or signature_set of kiosk_started Silent kiosks time of the latest entry of each kiosk Refused USB devices (BadUSB attempts), to alert on usb_device_blocked, by kinds; composite = true for a key that is also a keyboard

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The same indicators in a few SIEMs, as a starting point: index and field names depend on how the entries are received (here, the fields of the JSON entry at the top level).

Splunk (TCP input, sourcetype = _json; a JSON list is the field detections{}):

event=device_verdict | timechart span=1d count by verdict
event=device_verdict | stats count by kiosk
event=device_verdict | top limit=10 detections{}
event=device_verdict | stats avg(duration) perc95(duration) by kiosk
event=device_verdict verdict=not_verified | table _time kiosk report_id not_scanned
event=signatures_installed OR event=signatures_changed | stats latest(serial) by kiosk
event=usb_device_blocked | table _time kiosk usb_id model port kinds{} composite

Elastic (Logstash or Elastic Agent, json codec; ES|QL in Kibana):

FROM pandora-box-* | WHERE event == "device_verdict"
  | STATS keys = COUNT(*) BY verdict, day = DATE_TRUNC(1 day, @timestamp)
FROM pandora-box-* | WHERE event == "device_verdict" | MV_EXPAND detections
  | STATS seen = COUNT(*) BY detections | SORT seen DESC | LIMIT 10
FROM pandora-box-* | WHERE event == "usb_device_blocked"
  | KEEP @timestamp, kiosk, usb_id, model, port, kinds, composite

Graylog (Syslog TCP input; the JSON of the message decoded by a pipeline rule, then searches and aggregation widgets on event:device_verdict, grouped by verdict, kiosk or detections):

rule "PandoraBox JSON"
when
  starts_with(to_string($message.message), "{")
then
  set_fields(to_map(parse_json(to_string($message.message))));
end

Wazuh (decoded by its JSON decoder): Wazuh only indexes the entries that match a rule; a local rule per event to count, then dashboards on data.event in OpenSearch Dashboards. A refused USB device raises an alert (level 10, 12 for a key that is also another device):

<group name="pandora-box,">
  <rule id="100100" level="3">
    <decoded_as>json</decoded_as>
    <field name="event">^device_verdict$</field>
    <description>PandoraBox $(kiosk): key scanned, $(verdict)</description>
  </rule>
  <rule id="100110" level="10">
    <decoded_as>json</decoded_as>
    <field name="event">^usb_device_blocked$</field>
    <description>PandoraBox $(kiosk): USB device refused, $(usb_id) $(model) on port $(port)</description>
    <group>attack,badusb,</group>
  </rule>
  <rule id="100111" level="12">
    <if_sid>100110</if_sid>
    <field name="composite">^true$</field>
    <description>PandoraBox $(kiosk): USB key that is also a keyboard or another device (BadUSB)</description>
  </rule>
</group>

Grafana Loki (syslog receiver of Grafana Alloy; LogQL, whose json parser leaves the lists out, detections among them):

sum by (verdict) (count_over_time({app="pandora-box"} | json | event="device_verdict" [1d]))
avg_over_time({app="pandora-box"} | json | event="device_verdict" | unwrap duration [1d])
sum by (kiosk, usb_id) (count_over_time({app="pandora-box"} | json | event="usb_device_blocked" [1d]))

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
transport Default port tls 6514 Recommended: the certificate of the SIEM is verified (certificate authorities of ca, host name of host), TLS 1.2 at least tcp 514 Clear text, on a trusted network only udp 514 Clear text; a datagram may be lost without notice

The kiosk does not authenticate itself with a client certificate.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
The log file is the queue. The service saves the position of the last entry sent (/var/lib/pandora-box-siem/state.json): when the SIEM cannot be reached, it tries again (after 1 second, then twice longer each time, up to 1 minute) and sends every entry logged meanwhile, in order. The same applies when the service or the kiosk restarts. logrotate moves the log file every month: the service sends the end of the moved file before the new one, so an outage longer than a month loses the entries of the oldest month.

Syslog has no acknowledgment: over TCP and TLS, the entries sent just before a connection breaks may be lost, or sent twice when it is broken while they are sent. Over UDP, nothing is guaranteed.

docs.title: The service
docs.text:
pandora-box-siem.service (src/pandora_box/siem.py) follows the log file and sends its entries. It exits at once when [siem] is disabled.

  • The kiosk itself has no network (IPAddressDeny=any, no IP socket): it only writes the log file. The service runs as the pandora-box-siem user, without privileges and in a systemd sandbox, and the firewall lets that user out (TCP and UDP) besides the update service.
  • It reads the log file through the pandora-box-log group, the group of /var/log/pandora-box and of the files of the kiosk: it can read neither the scan reports nor the quarantine (/var/lib/pandora-box, mode 0700).
  • Its messages, connection lost and back, are in its journal: journalctl -u pandora-box-siem.

docs.title: Receivers
docs.text:
Wazuh: the manager receives syslog over TCP or UDP, without TLS, from the addresses it allows (<remote> of ossec.conf, connection syslog). With format = "json" and transport = "tcp", each entry reaches the JSON decoder of Wazuh as is; check the decoding with wazuh-logtest.

rsyslog, over TLS (packages rsyslog and rsyslog-gnutls):

global(
    DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/rsyslog.d/ca.pem"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile="/etc/rsyslog.d/siem.pem"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile="/etc/rsyslog.d/siem.key"
)
module(load="imtcp" StreamDriver.Name="gtls" StreamDriver.Mode="1"
       StreamDriver.AuthMode="anon")
input(type="imtcp" port="6514")

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
The service runs outside of the image too, with any configuration whose [siem] is enabled, here towards a local receiver:

nc -lk 5514 &
pandora-box-siem --config pandora-box.toml --state /tmp/siem-state.json

with host = "127.0.0.1", transport = "tcp" and port = 5514. The virtual machine test sends the logs of the kiosk to a syslog receiver of the test (Testing with QEMU).

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text: The detection engines of a kiosk only use a signed signature set, verified at each start. A set is installed from a signature update device (a USB key holding a set, for kiosks without network) or, when it is enabled, online. Without a valid set, the kiosk scans nothing: it shows NO VALID SIGNATURES and waits for a signature update device.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
On the computer that holds the update key, for instance every day:

export ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY=...
publish/publish.sh /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures /secure/update.key
cp -r /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures /media/$USER/KEY/

Insert the key into the kiosk: it installs the set, reloads its engines and asks to remove the key. An online kiosk does it by itself every 6 hours.

docs.title: Updating a kiosk
docs.text:
Copy a signed set into a pandora-box-signatures folder at the root of a USB key (vfat, exFAT, NTFS or ext4) and insert it into the kiosk. The kiosk verifies and installs the set, reloads its engines, then asks to remove the key: a signature update device is never scanned, so do not use it to carry other files.

The kiosk shows and logs the result (signatures_installed, signatures_refused with the reason, or signatures_not_newer). A set is only installed when it is newer than the installed one.

The kiosk warns when its signatures get old (see Signature freshness).

docs.title: Preparing a set
docs.text:
pandora-box-signatures publish downloads the signatures of every engine from their sources, checks that the engines of a kiosk can load them, then builds and signs a set (src/pandora_box/publish.py):

Source Files Notes clamav clamav/main.cvd, daily, bytecode updated by freshclam (incremental), which verifies their Cisco Talos signature yara-forge yara/yara-forge/yara-rules-core.yar YARA Forge "core" package, latest GitHub release signature-base yara/signature-base/*.yar opt-in: YARA Forge already includes its rules malwarebazaar malwarebazaar/malwarebazaar.sha256.bin full SHA-256 export, needs a free abuse.ch Auth-Key (ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY) hashlookup hashlookup/hashlookup-full.bloom about 1 GB, published monthly

The publication runs in a container holding freshclam, clamscan and the engines, for instance every day on the computer that holds the signing key:

export ABUSECH_AUTH_KEY=...
publish/publish.sh /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures /secure/update.key
cp -r /srv/pandora-box/pandora-box-signatures /media/KEY/

Downloads are HTTPS only and cached (--cache, default ~/.cache/pandora-box-signatures): a source that did not change (ETag, Last-Modified) is not downloaded again. Before signing, the set is loaded with the engines of the kiosk: the YARA rules must compile with YARA-X, the MalwareBazaar database and the Hashlookup filter must load, and clamscan must load the ClamAV databases. A set that fails is never signed, and the previous output folder is kept: a broken set, validly signed, would make every kiosk that installs it unable to scan. The set must contain the files of every engine enabled on the kiosks: a kiosk refuses to scan with a set that misses one.

The full set is about 1.2 GB (ClamAV about 115 MB, YARA Forge core 8 MB, Hashlookup 1 GB). With the full ClamAV databases, clamd uses about 1 GB of memory on the kiosk (measured in the test virtual machine). Signing uses openssl, so that the private key can stay in a hardware token (OpenSSL provider). The release key of the project and its storage are not defined yet.

The command also works on sets built by other means:

pandora-box-signatures build FOLDER --key update.key   # manifest.json + signature
pandora-box-signatures verify FOLDER --keys KEYS_FOLDER
pandora-box-signatures install FOLDER                   # by hand, on a kiosk

build and publish number the set with its creation date (YYYYMMDDHHMMSS) unless --serial is given.

docs.title: Online updates
docs.text:
A kiosk works offline by default. An image built with the profile online (Building the image) updates its signatures itself, from their sources: ClamAV (freshclam), YARA Forge, MalwareBazaar and Hashlookup, the sources of pandora-box-signatures publish. The profile brings DHCP on the wired network (IPv4), DNS (systemd-resolved, without LLMNR or mDNS), NTP (systemd-timesyncd, Time), freshclam, the pandora-box-update timer (every 6 hours, 5 minutes after boot), and a firewall that only lets out the update service (TCP), the log export to a SIEM (SIEM), DHCP, DNS and NTP. Nothing comes in but the answers to these connections. It enables the [updates] section of the configuration with every source:

[updates]
enabled = true
sources = ["clamav", "yara-forge", "malwarebazaar", "hashlookup"]
# Optional: a company mirror in place of a source ("clamav": a freshclam
# private mirror), and a proxy
# mirrors = { hashlookup = "https://mirror.example.org/hashlookup-full.bloom" }
# proxy = "http://proxy.example.org:3128"

The kiosk loads the new set the next time it is idle (between two devices): a scan is never interrupted. It logs signatures_changed and shows New signatures installed. Signature update devices are still accepted (a kiosk cut from the network, or signatures newer than the last download).

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
MalwareBazaar needs an abuse.ch Auth-Key (free account: https://auth.abuse.ch/). It is given at build time in image/credentials.toml (see image/credentials.toml.example; git ignores the file), and the profile installs it on the read-only root filesystem as a systemd credential, /etc/credstore/pandora-box.abusech-auth-key, readable by root only: systemd gives it to the update service alone (ImportCredential=). Without it, MalwareBazaar is not downloaded and its database is kept from the last signature update device.

Warning

An image built with credentials must not be published: anyone with the image or the disk of the kiosk can read them.

docs.title: A published set instead
docs.text:
A kiosk can also download a signed set published by pandora-box-signatures publish on a web server, in place of the sources: url (the folder of the set) instead of sources. It then needs no credential, and only installs a set signed with the update key, newer than the installed one, downloading only the files that changed.

The same service also installs online image updates (updates.image_url, see System updates).

docs.title: The update service
docs.text:
pandora-box-update.service runs in two steps (src/pandora_box/online.py):

  1. as the pandora-box-update user, which the firewall lets out, without privileges and in a systemd sandbox, it downloads the sources (with an HTTP cache, /var/lib/pandora-box-update/staging-sources: an unchanged source is not downloaded again; freshclam downloads the daily differences of ClamAV), checks that the engines load them, and builds a set in /var/lib/pandora-box-update/staging when they changed. The files of the sources it does not download are taken from the installed set;
  2. as root, without network, it signs the staged set with the key of the kiosk and installs it (install --staged): every check of a signature update device applies, the unchanged files are taken from the installed set.

The key of the kiosk is an Ed25519 key generated on the kiosk the first time (/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures/local-key/, the private key readable by root only). The kiosk trusts it besides the keys of its image: it verifies the installed set at each start, whoever signed it.

The downloads are HTTPS (a mirror configured in updates.mirrors may be HTTP); the ClamAV databases carry the signature of Cisco Talos, verified by freshclam. freshclam does not load the new databases to test them (TestDatabases no): clamd already holds them in memory, a kiosk has 2 GB. Redirects are only followed to HTTPS URLs, and the proxy of the environment is ignored: only updates.proxy is used.

docs.title: Signature sets
docs.text:
A signature set is a folder holding the signature files of the engines and a signed list of them (src/pandora_box/sigsets.py):

manifest.json          serial, creation date, and the SHA-256 and size of every file
manifest.json.sig      Ed25519 signature of manifest.json
clamav/main.cvd        ClamAV databases (clamd reads this folder)
clamav/daily.cvd
malwarebazaar/malwarebazaar.sha256.bin
hashlookup/hashlookup-full.bloom
yara/yara-forge/yara-rules-core.yar

The paths are those of the default configuration (/var/lib/pandora-box-signatures/current/...). The manifest.json of a subfolder (written by pandora-box-signatures publish) gives the source, version and date of its files; without it, the date of a file is the creation date of the set, used for the signature freshness warnings.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
• The kiosk trusts the Ed25519 public keys (*.pem) of signatures.keys, /usr/share/pandora-box/keys/ in the image: they are part of the root filesystem, protected by dm-verity and Secure Boot. The update key is separate from the image signing key: sets are signed far more often.
  • The signature is verified with openssl, on the exact bytes of the manifest, before anything else of the set is read.
  • A set is only installed when its serial is higher than the installed one: an older set, even validly signed, is refused (no rollback).
  • Every file is copied with its size and SHA-256 checked against the manifest; files not listed are ignored; paths are plain names (no .., no hidden name) and links are never followed.
  • The set is installed next to the current one, then a current link is switched atomically: an interrupted update changes nothing. The previous set is kept.
  • At each start, the kiosk verifies the installed set again (signature, then every file) and refuses engine files that are not part of it (signatures.verify). Without a valid set, it scans nothing: it shows NO VALID SIGNATURES and only accepts a signature update device. A new kiosk therefore starts by asking for one.

ClamAV databases (.cvd) are also signed by Cisco Talos and verified by clamd. clamd reads the clamav folder of the installed set (DatabaseDirectory), and is restarted when it changes.

docs.title: Development keys
docs.text:
image/build.sh generates a development key pair, image/update.key and image/update.pem (ignored by git), when they do not exist: the image trusts update.pem, and the test image installs a set signed with update.key. Never use them for a kiosk.

On a development computer, pandora-box-signatures publish without --key builds an unsigned set and prints the matching configuration, with verify = false in [signatures].

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: What PandoraBox protects, against whom, how, and what it does not cover. It describes the kiosk image built from this repository, on the validated hardware, installed as in Initial installation.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
A kiosk takes USB keys of unknown origin, scans their files with several engines and removes the dangerous ones before the keys are used on a workstation. It assumes that every key is hostile: not only its files, but also its filesystem and the USB device itself. Everything that reads the key is confined, the system cannot be changed without the release keys, and the kiosk tells the user when it could not check a key entirely.

PandoraBox reduces the risk; it does not remove it. A file that no engine detects is reported clean, and a key whose firmware is malicious can show other files to the workstation. Keep the protections of the workstations.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text: Asset Why it matters The verdict shown to the user A key reported clean is used on a workstation: a wrong "clean" is the main failure The integrity of the kiosk system A compromised kiosk could report every key clean, or infect the keys it scans The signature sets Old or forged signatures detect nothing The release keys (Secure Boot, update) Whoever holds them decides what a kiosk boots and trusts Scan reports, logs and quarantine Names and hashes of the files of the users, copies of malware The workstations and the network behind the kiosk What the kiosk is there to protect

docs.title: Attackers
docs.text:
Attacker Means Goal A user, unknowingly A key infected elsewhere None: the most common case, and the reason for the kiosk A crafted key Malicious files, crafted filesystem, partition table or USB descriptors, a device that is not a storage device (BadUSB) Pass malware off as clean; take over the kiosk A passer-by Physical access to the kiosk for minutes: the scanning ports, the screen, the enclosure Change the system, read the reports and the quarantine The network An online kiosk talks to update servers, NTP and a SIEM Forge signatures, delay updates, read the logs The supply chain Debian packages, signature sources (ClamAV, YARA Forge, abuse.ch, CIRCL), the build machine Plant a backdoor in an image or a signature set

The administrators who build the images and hold the release keys are trusted.

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text:
USB key (hostile)
   │  USB descriptors ─────────► USBGuard: only mass storage, touchscreen by its rule
   │  partition table, vfat ───► kernel of the kiosk
   │  NTFS, exFAT, ext4 ───────► FUSE driver, sandboxed (pandora-box-scan, no capability)
   ▼
 kiosk process (root, hardened systemd service)
   │  lists, opens and hashes the files; never interprets their content
   │  passes each file as a descriptor, gets validated JSON back
   ▼
 scan workers, one per engine, sandboxed (bubblewrap, no network, seccomp)
   libmagic, YARA-X, heuristics, clamd client  ─►  clamd (own sandbox, no network)

 Signature sets, image updates, maintenance requests (hostile until verified)
   └─► Ed25519 signature checked against the keys of the read-only root filesystem
 Boot: firmware ─► systemd-boot ─► kernel image, signed (Secure Boot) ─► root on dm-verity

docs.title: A crafted key against the kiosk
docs.text: Threat Mitigations A USB device that is a keyboard, a network adapter or a serial port (BadUSB) USBGuard authorizes no device before it starts, then only mass storage; keyboards and mice are blocked; no USB network, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or serial drivers (USB devices); each refused device is logged and sent to the SIEM (usb_device_blocked) A crafted filesystem exploiting a kernel driver NTFS, exFAT and ext4 are read by FUSE drivers in the sandbox, the kernel has no driver for NTFS and exFAT; only vfat stays in the kernel (Filesystem drivers) A file exploiting a parser (libmagic, YARA-X, ClamAV) Each engine in its own worker, sandboxed: no network, no device, no data of the kiosk, dedicated user, system call filter; clamd in its own sandbox; a worker only reports its own engine, the kiosk combines the results (Scan worker sandbox) Links, special files, deep trees, huge keys, decompression bombs The inventory never follows a link nor leaves the device; limits on file size, file count and depth; beyond them the key is not verified Writing to the key during the scan, an ext4 journal replay The key is mounted read-only on a read-only block device; an ext4 key whose journal needs a replay is refused A worker or driver that crashes or hangs Timeouts and watchdogs; the files concerned are not fully scanned and the key is reported not verified, never clean A key swapped between the scan and the cleaning A file is only removed if its SHA-256 is still the scanned one

docs.title: Malware passed off as clean
docs.text: Threat Mitigations Malware unknown to one engine Five engines: ClamAV, YARA-X (YARA Forge), MalwareBazaar, Hashlookup, heuristics; a malicious verdict from any engine wins A known file used as a disguise A Hashlookup hit means "known", not "benign": content engines still scan it by default Encrypted archives and documents, files beyond the limits Not scannable: reported, and the key is not verified (scan.on_error = "block") Documents with macros or active content, programs disguised as documents Reported suspicious, removed like malicious files by default (scan.suspicious = "block") Old signatures Freshness warnings on the screen; signature sets are updated offline or online

docs.title: The system of the kiosk
docs.text: Threat Mitigations Changing the system on the disk Read-only EROFS root filesystem checked by dm-verity, its root hash in the kernel image signed for Secure Boot; the firmware only trusts the certificate of the image; a modified block cannot be read Booting something else BIOS supervisor password, Secure Boot in custom mode, no boot loader menu, no keyboard read at boot (Initial installation) Logging in No login program, no root password, no console, Ctrl-Alt-Del masked; logs leave through a maintenance request signed with the update key Installing an older or forged version Image updates and signature sets are signed with the update key and must be newer than the installed ones; A/B slots with automatic return to the previous version Kernel attacks from a compromised process Lockdown confidentiality, no unprivileged user namespaces, eBPF or userfaultfd, unused kernel modules removed, IOMMU

docs.title: The network (online kiosks)
docs.text: Threat Mitigations Forged or replayed signatures from a malicious server Sets built on the kiosk from the sources are checked by the engines, then signed with a key generated on the kiosk; published sets must carry a trusted signature and a newer serial; ClamAV databases are also signed by Cisco Talos Other traffic from a compromised process Firewall: everything dropped except DHCP, DNS, NTP, the update service and the SIEM export, each allowed by its system user; the kiosk and the workers have no network Reading the exported logs Syslog over TLS by default, with the certificate authorities of the SIEM A fake server receiving the copied keys, or reading them on the way (airgap) The host key of the SSH server must be listed in the image, never trusted on first use; the copy service has its own user and reads nothing of the kiosk but the clean files staged for it

docs.title: Supply chain and releases
docs.text: Threat Mitigations A tampered release Release keys on two YubiKeys; checksums signed with the update key; reproducible builds: anyone can rebuild a release from its tag and compare it (Releases) A tampered package Debian packages from snapshot.debian.org, pinned at the time of the tag; Python packages pinned by hash; a software bill of materials (CycloneDX) per release

docs.title: What PandoraBox does not cover
docs.text:
• Undetected malware. A new or targeted file that no engine knows is reported clean. The kiosk is one layer: keep the protections of the workstations.
  • A key with malicious firmware. A USB key can show some content to the kiosk and other content to the workstation, or change once the kiosk has ejected it. No scan can rule that out: only trusted keys do.
  • The USB and storage stack of the kernel. The kernel still parses the USB descriptors, the partition table and vfat. A kernel flaw there is outside every sandbox.
  • A compromised FUSE driver or engine cannot take over the kiosk, but it can hide files or report a wrong verdict for its own engine.
  • The kiosk process itself runs as root: it lists the files and hashes them, and draws their names on the screen (FreeType); a flaw there is not sandboxed.
  • Physical access beyond the scanning ports. Opening the enclosure gives access to the disk: /var is not encrypted (no TPM), so the reports, the logs and the quarantine can be read. A station that copies to a server keeps none of them, nor the folders of the keys on the server: see A stolen kiosk. Lost BIOS password, disconnected intrusion switch or reachable internal ports defeat the boot protections.
  • The release keys. Whoever holds the YubiKeys and their PIN can build an image that the kiosks boot and trust.
  • The clock of an offline kiosk. The freshness warnings rely on the clock of the computer.
  • Denial of service. A key can make a scan long or fail; the limits and timeouts keep the kiosk available, the key is not verified.
  • Encrypted devices, smartphones and MTP devices are not supported.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• The kiosk runs an image built from this repository, with release keys kept as described in Releases.
  • It is installed as in Initial installation: BIOS password, Secure Boot with the certificate of the image only, enclosure that only exposes the scanning ports.
  • Its signatures are updated regularly.
  • Users bring the cleaned keys to workstations that keep their own protections.

To report a vulnerability, follow the security policy.

docs.title: System updates
docs.text:
The system of a kiosk is read-only: it is updated as a whole, with a new image, never file by file. The disk has two system slots (A/B): the update is written to the free slot while the kiosk runs, and the previous version stays until the new one has booted successfully. The configuration and the theme are part of the image: changing them is also an update.

The signatures are updated separately, far more often: see Signatures.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
image/build.sh                    # new version, same keys and profile as the kiosk
image/package-update.sh image/mkosi.output/pandora-box.raw update image/update.key
cp -r update /media/$USER/KEY/pandora-box-image

Insert the key into the kiosk: it installs the update and restarts on the new version.

docs.title: Building an update
docs.text:
Build a new version with the same keys as the installed image (its version is the time of the build: newer than the running one), and with the same profile, then package it:

image/build.sh
image/package-update.sh image/mkosi.output/pandora-box.raw update image/update.key

update/ holds the partitions of slot A of the new image (compressed with xz, the format that systemd-sysupdate of Debian 13 decompresses), named with their UUID, the unified kernel image, and a manifest signed with the update key (the format of the signature sets, content image, serial = version). About 215 MB, of which 40 MB for the kernel image.

Two keys protect the update: the update key decides what is installed, the Secure Boot key decides what can boot (the kernel image is signed and holds the root hash of its slot). An update built with other keys is refused, or does not boot.

docs.title: Installing from a USB key
docs.text:
Copy update/ as pandora-box-image/ at the root of a USB key (vfat, exFAT, NTFS or ext4) and insert it into the kiosk (updates.image_from_devices, on by default).

The kiosk verifies the signature, that the version is newer than the running one and every file, copies them to /var/lib/pandora-box-image, then systemd-sysupdate writes the partitions to the free slot and the kernel image to the ESP with 3 boot tries (pandora-box_2+3-0.efi), and the kiosk restarts. The running version is never overwritten; the device is not scanned.

One key can hold a maintenance request, a signature set and an image update: the kiosk handles them in that order, each verified on its own; the image update comes last as it restarts the kiosk.

docs.title: Online
docs.text: With the profile online (Building the image) and updates.image_url, the URL of a published update/ folder, pandora-box-update.service downloads a newer update as its unprivileged user (every file checked), then installs it as root without network (pandora-box-image install), with the same checks as an update device. The kiosk restarts on the new version when it is idle (between two devices): a scan is never interrupted.

docs.title: If the new version fails
docs.text:
The new version is kept (systemd-bless-boot) once boot-complete.target is reached, which requires the kiosk to be ready (Type=notify). A boot that fails restarts: kernel panic (panic=10), failure in the initrd (its emergency shell restarts, image/mkosi.images/initrd/), or no boot-complete.target in 15 minutes. After 3 failed tries, systemd-boot boots the previous version again; the data (/var: reports, quarantine, logs, signatures) is shared by the versions.

boot-entries.txt and boots.txt of a maintenance device show the installed versions and the boots.

docs.title: What is not updated
docs.text: The ESP is not part of the image updates: systemd-boot, its settings and the Secure Boot keys enrolled in the firmware stay as installed. Changing the Secure Boot key needs a new installation.

docs.title: Testing with QEMU
docs.text: The image is tested in a QEMU/KVM virtual machine, without the reference hardware: UEFI firmware (OVMF) with Secure Boot, an empty USB 3 controller, and USB keys inserted and removed while the kiosk runs, which triggers the same udev events as a real device. QEMU runs in the build container: only Docker is needed, and /dev/kvm for speed.

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
image/build-test.sh   # the test image and three image updates
image/vm.sh test      # automated test, about 7 minutes with KVM
image/vm.sh run       # interactive machine, kiosk screen on VNC localhost:0

Note

Hostile samples should only ever be copied into key images, never onto the development desktop.

docs.title: Test profile
docs.text:
--profile test builds pandora-box-test.raw, for the virtual machine tests only, never for a kiosk. It includes the profile online, and adds:

  • a test-only signature set, generated from image/vm/corpus.py, signed with the development update key and installed (serial 1): a ClamAV database that detects the EICAR test file, a MalwareBazaar database, a Hashlookup filter and a YARA rule, each detecting one file of the test key;
  • the matching configuration, with every engine enabled, and online updates from http://10.0.2.2:8080/ (the build container, seen from the QEMU user network);
  • a root shell without password on the virtio console (hvc0), and kernel messages on the serial port;
  • kiosk-screen, which prints the texts of the kiosk screen in that shell (the graphical interface logs them, display_screen events at the DEBUG level);
  • a USBGuard rule for the touch tablet of the virtual machine (QEMU usb-tablet, /etc/usbguard/rules.d/50-vm-test.conf): the test confirms a cleaning with a touch. The keyboard of the virtual machines is not a USB device.

image/build-test.sh builds the test image (version 1) and three signed image updates to newer versions (image/mkosi.output/updates/), for the A/B update test.

docs.title: Automated test
docs.text:
image/build-test.sh
image/vm.sh test

The test boots the test image in QEMU (KVM when /dev/kvm is writable, otherwise much slower emulation), with UEFI firmware (OVMF) where the image signing certificate is enrolled (Secure Boot enabled), and an empty USB 3 controller. It plays the whole user workflow, through QMP and the shell on the virtio console:

  1. the kiosk starts with its five engines and the signature set 1, verified, and no systemd unit fails;
  2. the scan workers (one engine each) run in their sandbox (user, capabilities, no_new_privs, seccomp, network namespace, no device or kiosk data in their file system); Secure Boot is enabled, the kernel is locked down and the root filesystem is on dm-verity;
  3. the root filesystem is read-only EROFS, and /var was grown to fill the 8 GB disk of the machine;
  4. an emulated USB key (a vfat disk image holding the corpus) is inserted, which triggers the same udev events as a real device;
  5. each file gets the expected verdict from the expected engine;
  6. the cleaning is confirmed with a touch on the kiosk screen; the infected files are quarantined (checked against their SHA-256) and removed from the key, which is ejected;
  7. the key is removed: only the clean files are left on it;
  8. the cleaned key is inserted again and reported clean;
  9. keys of the other filesystems go through the same scan and cleaning, then are reported clean: exfat, NTFS, ext4 (its files private to their owner, as on the key of a Linux user), each read by its FUSE driver, and a key with an MBR partition table and a vfat partition; a key on EROFS (a filesystem the kernel mounts, but not allowed) is refused; a vfat key with a cut cluster chain and an ext4 key whose group descriptors are overwritten are mounted, but a file or the folders cannot be read: the key is reported not verified (image/vm/keys.py; exfat and NTFS have no tool writing files without mounting them: they are formatted in the container, then filled by the FUSE drivers of the machine, the kiosk stopped);
  10. a signature update key with a newer set (serial 2) is installed, the engines are reloaded and the new sample it detects is found; a modified set, a set signed with another key and an older set are refused; a newer set published on an HTTP server by the test is downloaded by the update service (only its changed file), installed and loaded by the idle kiosk, and only the update service user can open a network connection (systemd-timesyncd alone sends NTP requests); the log entries of the kiosk are sent to a syslog receiver of the test ([siem]), by the SIEM export user, who cannot read the reports; with the copy to a server enabled ([airgap], an SFTP server of the test), the clean files of a key are copied by the copy service user, the key keeps its malicious files and gets its identifier, then a file removed from the key is deleted from the server; an emulated USB keyboard and network adapter are blocked by USBGuard (no input device, no network interface) and the excluded drivers are not in the image; the kernel settings, the firewall and the service sandboxes are in place;
  11. after a reboot, the scan reports are still there, the root filesystem is unchanged and the signature set 5 is verified at start; a key pressed while the firmware and the boot loader start does not open the boot loader menu;
  12. an image update key to version 2 is inserted: the kiosk installs it in the free slot and restarts, version 2 boots from slot B and is kept (its UKI loses its boot counter), with the same data; version 3, published on an HTTP server by the test, is downloaded and installed by the update service, then the idle kiosk restarts on it and it is kept; finally a version 4 whose root filesystem is modified is installed from a key: it fails 3 boots (dm-verity, the initrd restarts) and systemd-boot goes back to version 3.

Two more machines boot the same image:

  • with a block of the root filesystem modified on the disk (a canary file of the test image): it cannot be read and the kernel reports the corruption;
